title: AWS Textract Pricing 2026: Cost per 1,000 Pages
summary: AWS Textract pricing includes separate per-page costs for document extraction, queries, adaptations, and advanced features, helping you estimate spending.
body_markdown:
## Connect Textract to a workflow with Activepieces


Do not expect Activepieces to make Textract cheaper: the $1.50 to $50 per 1,000 pages stays exactly as AWS sets it, so these charges apply regardless of which workflow platform you use.


It supplies the trigger and the hand-off that Textract leaves to you, and that gap is where hidden labour and accidental re-runs creep into a client's bill.


Once you have last month's tally by client and document type, the next question is what moves each file into Textract and each result out of it. Every manual step there is time you either bill or absorb.


### What Textract does not automate


Give Textract a document and it returns text, tables or fields. It doesn't notice that a file arrived, decide which feature to call, check the output, or put the result in front of the person who approves it. Someone or something has to do that.


If that someone is a staffer dragging files into a console, you're paying for the extraction twice: once to AWS and once in salary. If it's a script nobody owns, the risk is quieter.


When a failed run is retried by hand, the same pages are processed again, and the repeat lands on the shared account. No single client sees it, and the clients with messy scans end up subsidised by the ones with clean PDFs.


What Activepieces does here is the plumbing around Textract, not the extraction.


It is a workflow builder with 747 integrations in an MIT-licensed core, which connects triggers, apps and custom HTTP calls, meaning you probably won't need custom code for most services you want to integrate.


The per-page price, the feature you choose and the pages you re-run stay exactly as AWS meters them.


### A trigger-to-spreadsheet workflow


You build the flow below in the Activepieces canvas in ten steps, so each step is a discrete configuration block, and because flows are unlimited on every plan, including free, you can give each document type its own.


It runs from a schedule trigger through Google Sheets, a loop, a date helper and an HTTP request.


After that come two AI steps, a Sheets insert, a router with a branch and an Otherwise path, and a Gmail send, so AI processes your data before it reaches the routing decision.


Take from the flow the shape, not the exact steps: one trigger, one loop over new items, one call out, one write-back, and a router that separates clean results from ones needing a human.


For Textract, swap the trigger for a watch on a folder or inbox and point the HTTP request at the Textract API with the one feature that document type needs.


Write each result to a sheet row tagged with client and document type. That tag is what lets you bill by feature next month, and it's what your calculator lines were built to match.


Use the router to catch low-confidence or empty extractions and send those to a person before anything is resubmitted. A deliberate, logged re-run is a cost you can quote; a silent retry is one you can't.
